label: Warner Bros.
rationale: Mwandishi is the first album by the working band Hancock named for his own Swahili name: it is 'the first album to officially feature Hancock's Mwandishi sextet', with Bennie Maupin, Eddie Henderson, Julian Priester, Buster Williams and Billy Hart, recorded in a single session on New Year's Eve 1970, every member taking a Swahili name for the project [S1,S5] (obs). Rating evidence is enthusiast-strong but not a critics' lock: AllMusic gives it five stars, the Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide three, the Penguin Guide to Jazz Recordings three [S1 review box] (obs) — thinner than a consensus-core record, and the case has to be made on lineage instead. Lineage, which is the test this gate applies rather than the genre label: the record stands between the two Hancocks the canon already holds, and jazzdisco's session index carries the identical sextet forward into Crossings (1972) and Sextant (1973) [S2] (obs), so this is a documented continuing ensemble rather than a one-off; AllMusic's style tags for the album — Fusion, Jazz-Funk, Post-Bop, Piano Jazz [S3] — describe electric texture carried inside long modal/post-bop forms, not backbeat rock. Session gravity: a settled sextet of first-call players, with Leon 'Ndugu' Chancler, José 'Chepito' Areas and Ronnie Montrose added as the 'also appearing' guests on the opening track only [S4,S2] (obs). It still plays: 'Ostinato (Suite for Angela)', built on a 15/8 cycle, and the 21-minute 'Wandering Spirit Song' are the pieces the Mwandishi band is remembered by [S1,S7] (inf). Boundary: this is a fusion-gate arrival under the rubric's opened-gate rule (fusion/free-jazz/ECM admitted 2026-07-28, arrivals lean scope_call or contested); the argument offered is continuity with the post-bop Hancock already in the canon, never the merit of fusion as a genre. John rules.

personnel_record.notes: Single session. Hancock's own discography gives the specific day — December 31, 1970, 'recorded in a single session on New Year's Eve' (S5) — and jazzdisco says 'December, 1970' (S2); Wikipedia and one review say January 1971 (S1, S7). The December 1970 date is recorded here, the conflict preserved. Album durations differ by pressing: Wikipedia lists 13:10 / 10:22 / 21:26, the original 1971 LP as entered on Discogs 13:05 / 10:01 / 21:23. herbiehancock.com's credit block (S5) additionally lists Bernard Purdie, Johnny Coles and Joe Farrell, whom no session-level source (jazzdisco, Wikipedia, AllMusic, Discogs) places on these sessions; treated as a credits-page discrepancy rather than personnel, and flagged rather than dropped. Chancler, Areas and Montrose are 'also appearing' on 'Ostinato (Suite for Angela)' only (S4, S2).

scope_check.boundary_note: The opened fusion gate and its bridge test are in play: does the electric ensemble extend post-bop/modal practice sufficiently to serve this canon? The recording-date dispute does not affect eligibility, and the 1973+ continuity-band rule does not apply.

ballot.case_for: Mwandishi documents the founding statement of a sustained working sextet, with Hancock, Maupin, Henderson, Priester, Williams and Hart continuing together into Crossings and Sextant (S1, S2, S7). Its extended forms, electric-piano textures and collective improvisation offer a persuasive bridge from post-bop/modal exploration into electric jazz rather than treating rock backbeat as the organizing principle; AllMusic's Post-Bop and Piano Jazz tags support that reading (S3). The ensemble's gravity and the contrasting worlds of 'Ostinato' and the side-long 'Wandering Spirit Song' give the album distinctive discovery value, beyond merely documenting an early fusion experiment.
ballot.case_against: The supplied reception evidence does not establish broad canonical consensus: AllMusic's five-star rating sits beside three-star assessments from Penguin and the Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide, reported through S1 rather than directly sourced reviews. Being the sextet's first statement does not establish that it is its definitive one; the dossier documents continuity into Crossings and Sextant but does not demonstrate why this album is the strongest anchor for that trajectory. Its expansive, sometimes diffuse electric improvisation may also be less immediately illuminating for this personal discovery canon, while claims of lasting influence and listening durability remain less securely sourced than the session history.
ballot.disagreement: Both references agree on scope_call and strong, with no substantive scope disagreement. They differ in emphasis: Reference 1 treats the founding sextet document as a defining statement, while Reference 2 questions whether it is an embryonic statement better represented by Sextant; the dossier does not settle that comparative judgment.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes John give Mwandishi strong listening priority as a fusion-bridge candidate and assess whether this founding statement best represents the sextet's contribution.
